name: Colosseum, Rome
label: Colosseum
camera_source: Commons cluster (46 photos). Moved 84 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 110 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1834818: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Colosseum' (229 m across).
notes: 'colosseum' alone counts other venues; only 'rome'/'italy' phrases counted. Also on the Rome map.

text.description:
The Colosseum is an elliptical amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, just east of the Roman Forum. It is the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built, and it is still the largest standing amphitheatre in the world. Work began under Emperor Vespasian in AD 72 and finished in AD 80 under his successor and heir, Titus, with further changes made later under Domitian. The walls are built of travertine, Roman concrete and tuff, a volcanic rock. You can see how the stone has weathered, and where earthquakes and stone robbers have taken whole sections away.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear. The curved rows of arches repeat round the whole building, and the broken outer wall shows the layers behind it. That gives you strong patterns, depth and a real sense of age. The sources estimate that it held between 50,000 and 80,000 spectators, with an average crowd of about 65,000. Try a wide shot that shows how big it is, then a closer shot of the arches or the worn stone.

Expect people in most shots, as it is one of Rome's most popular tourist attractions. Use them to show scale, or wait a moment for a gap. Hold the phone steady and keep the horizon level so the arches don't lean.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Rome, just east of the Roman Forum, in the low valley between the Caelian, Esquiline and Palatine hills. The map marks the middle of the Colosseum's outline, which is 229 metres across.
text.directions_text: Start from Colosseo Metro station, the nearest station. The Colosseum is 143 metres to the south-east of it, about 2 minutes on foot. Cavour Metro station is a longer walk: the Colosseum is 506 metres to the south of it, about 8 minutes on foot. Walk west towards the building and stop when it fills your view the way you want. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the curve of the walls into one frame, because you are close. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of a section of arches. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as the arches and the worn stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Colosseo (south or front side of the piazza, facing the main facade). The whole outer facade of the amphitheatre filling the frame, with the arches and street life of the piazza below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the arches up with the horizontal lines to keep the building straight. Leave some sky above the top edge so the outline reads clearly. Include a few people at the bottom of the frame to show the scale. For a detail shot, fill the frame with a run of arches and let the rhythm do the work.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and texture. Live Photos can help if people walk through the frame, because you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the side facing you should catch the low sun. Around sunset, try night mode or a warm-toned shot as the light fades.

text.access_note: Walking round the outside is usually possible in the open area, but going inside is likely to be ticketed and controlled, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter than the rest of the day at the Colosseum.
From the stand-here point, the side of the building facing east should catch the low morning sun, while the afternoon light may come from behind the building.
From the stand-here point, the building is close enough that the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps to fit more into the frame.
The area around the outside of the Colosseum is usually open to walk around, while entry inside is likely to be ticketed and controlled.

name: Tre Cime di Lavaredo, Dolomites
label: Tre Cime
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (2026-11-11T02:00).
notes: Dolomites searches counted here: one of their best-known views.

text.description:
The Tre Cime di Lavaredo, also called the Drei Zinnen, are three blocky, battlement-like peaks in the Sexten Dolomites. Seen from east to west they are Cima Piccola, Cima Grande and Cima Ovest. The tallest, Cima Grande, reaches 2,999 metres, with Cima Ovest at 2,973 metres and Cima Piccola at 2,857 metres. Together they are among the best-known mountain groups in the Alps, and the surrounding area has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2009.

They photograph well because the three towers stand side by side with nothing in front of them but open alpine ground, so the whole group fits into one tidy frame. The pale rock stands out against sky, and the sheer walls look huge even on a small screen. Cima Grande was first climbed on 21 August 1869, which gives you a nice story to tell with your picture.

The phone icon on the map is about 860 m north-east of the subject. That is close enough to feel their scale, while the whole group still sits in one frame. Keep the horizon level and include some foreground path or grass to give a sense of size. Take a few frames over several minutes, because mountain weather here can change fast, with fog or wind arriving quickly even in summer. Dress warmly and wear proper shoes for the walk.
text.geographic_location: The Tre Cime stand in the Sexten Dolomites in north-eastern Italy, on the border between South Tyrol and the province of Belluno. They lie about 15 km north-east of Cortina d'Ampezzo in a straight line, with the town of Toblach to the north-west.
text.directions_text: Start from the nearest town and travel by car or bus towards Misurina. From Misurina a toll road leads to Rifugio Auronzo. From Rifugio Auronzo a wide hiking trail runs east past Rifugio Lavaredo to Forcella Lavaredo (Paternsattel); the viewpoint is just beyond the saddle. The phone icon on the map is about 860 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there; on the mountain, follow the marked trail rather than the straight line.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From the viewpoint the peaks are just under 1 km away. Start with the default lens (1x) to take in all three towers with the path and slopes below them. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more foreground and sky, and telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of one summit, such as Cima Grande.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 860 m north-east of the subject, at the viewpoint just above Forcella Lavaredo (Paternsattel), at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. The three north faces line up in front of you, Cima Piccola nearest, Cima Grande in the middle and Cima Ovest on the right.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the base of the peaks on the lower third line, with the sky taking the upper two thirds. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Add a bit of path, rock or grass at the bottom edge for scale. Try one wide shot and one tighter shot of a single peak.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rock face to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour and the pale rock does not wash out. Try a panorama if you want the whole ridge, holding the phone steady and moving slowly. Wipe the lens first, as cold and damp air can smear it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower, usually gives more shape and colour to the rock than the flat light of midday. Weather here changes quickly, so check the forecast before setting out and be ready to shoot when the cloud breaks.

text.access_note: This is open mountain terrain, and the road up to Rifugio Auronzo is a toll road, so check the official site before you go for road, parking and hut details.
claims_not_in_sources: Low sun in the early morning or late afternoon usually gives more shape and colour to the rock than midday light.
The stand-here point lies north-east of the peaks on the walking routes beyond Rifugio Auronzo towards Paternsattel.

text.description: Positano is a small town on the Amalfi Coast, in the province of Salerno in Campania. It can photograph well on a phone, because buildings give you colour, texture and a sense of height, and any water in view gives a simple backdrop. Start with a wide view that shows the houses and, if it is visible, the sea. Then move in on smaller details such as doorways, balconies, shutters and plants. If people pass through your frame, wait for a gap. Keep your phone steady against your body, or rest your arms on a wall. Take a few frames of each view and choose the best one later. Watch your footing while looking at the screen, and step aside so others can pass. If you want to visit a particular viewpoint, beach or paid attraction, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Positano is on the Amalfi Coast in the province of Salerno, in the Campania region of southern Italy. The spot is in Positano, in the Campania region of Italy.
text.directions_text: Positano has no railway station. The usual ways in are the SITA bus along the Amalfi Coast road, from Sorrento (which has a Circumvesuviana train station) or from Amalfi, and seasonal ferries from Amalfi, Salerno and Sorrento; check current timetables before you go. From the bus stops or the ferry pier, walk into town. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall view of the town. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in narrow lanes or when you want more of the buildings in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out groups of buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and, if the sea or horizon is in view, place its line on a lower third line. Let the buildings fill the rest of the frame. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a second shot, step in and frame a doorway or balcony with a small bit of colour in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and pale walls keep their detail. Try a Live Photo while people walk past, as you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, but the town can be photographed at any time of day.

text.access_note: Positano is a town with public streets, but check the official site before you go for any specific viewpoint, beach or paid attraction.

name: Pompeii
label: Pompeii
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Pompeii'.

text.description:
Pompeii was a Roman town near Naples, in Campania, that was buried under 4 to 6 metres of volcanic ash and pumice when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD. Because the ash sealed so much in place, you can walk streets, look into houses and shops, and see decoration that has survived for nearly 2,000 years. The town was home to roughly 11,000 people, and the ancient city covered about 64 to 67 hectares. It is also one of the most visited places in Italy, with around 2.5 million visitors a year.

It photographs well because of the long, straight stone-paved streets, the low walls and doorways, and the open sky above roofless buildings. These give your pictures a sense of depth and scale. Start with a wide view to show the layout, then move in on smaller details such as worn paving, doorways and wall surfaces. Walk slowly and check your background before each shot, because other visitors will often be in the frame. Keep a hand free for the phone and watch your footing on uneven stones.
text.geographic_location: Pompeii lies in the municipality of Pompei, in the Campania region, close to Naples and about 8 km from Mount Vesuvius.
text.directions_text: Start from Pompei Scavi - Villa dei Misteri railway station, which is the nearest station given. Pompeii is about 459 m east of it, roughly 7 minutes on foot (about 7 minutes on foot), so head east. Walk from the phone icon on the map to Pompeii in about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking street scenes. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for narrow streets and large open spaces. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as doorways, wall textures and far-off buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a paved street or a row of walls with one of the lines, so the eye is led into the picture. Keep the horizon level. Hold the phone low for more paving in the foreground, then take a second shot at eye level. Try to leave a gap between visitors so the ruins stay the main subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main wall or building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Use panorama for wide views, and move slowly and steadily as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually more comfortable and often gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh on pale stone, so look for shade or shoot along the streets.

text.access_note: This is an archaeological site that may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bellagio and Varenna, Lake Como
label: Lake Como
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/46618: large area 'Varenna' (6978 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Varenna is a small lakeside village on Lake Como, with Bellagio facing it across the water. The village is the easier half to photograph up close. Houses crowd down to the water's edge, and the lake behind them gives each frame a clear foreground, middle and background. Varenna was founded by local fishermen in AD 769, and that fishing-village layout is still the main reason it photographs well: narrow, packed buildings with the mountains rising behind. Villa Monastero, on the edge of the village, began as a Cistercian monastery in the 11th or 12th century and is now a museum and botanical garden. The Castello di Vezio is one of Varenna's main sights. Both are worth keeping in the frame or adding to your walk. Use the phone icon on the map as your starting position, then move along the waterfront a few steps at a time. Small changes in position shift how the buildings overlap and how much of the far shore you see. For a phone, the simplest approach is a wide frame that includes the water, the village and some sky, followed by a tighter shot of a single row of houses or a boat. Watch the edges of the frame for railings and signs, and keep the horizon level. Bellagio is on the far shore, so a zoomed shot across the water works well when the air is clear.
text.geographic_location: Varenna is on Lake Como, in the Province of Lecco in Lombardy, about 60 km north of Milan (around 46.0108 N, 9.2838 E). Bellagio is across the lake in the Province of Como.
text.directions_text: Start from Varenna-Esino-Perledo railway station. The village is about 513 m to the south of the station, which is about 8 minutes on foot. Walk south towards the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the village and water together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the buildings and want the whole frontage in one shot. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details on the far shore, such as Bellagio's waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Walk a little to either side to change how the buildings line up against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, so either the water or the sky takes up most of the frame. Include something in the foreground, such as a railing, boat or stone edge, to give depth. Try a wider shot first, then a closer crop of a single row of houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the village to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or water looks washed out. If the air is hazy and you are zooming across the lake, hold the phone steady with both hands and take a couple of shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the waterfront. Midday sun can flatten the colours and cause glare on the water.

text.access_note: The village waterfront appears to be open public space, but Villa Monastero and the Castello di Vezio may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
label: Leaning Tower
camera_source: Commons cluster (218 photos). Moved 63 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 130 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12982355: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Leaning Tower of Pisa' (23 m across).

text.description: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is the freestanding bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, and it stands in Cathedral Square (Piazza del Duomo) beside the cathedral and the baptistery. It photographs well because the lean is obvious at a glance. The white marble tower, with its stacked rows of arches, also stands out against the open lawn and the sky around it. The lean is nearly four degrees, and it comes from soft ground under a shallow foundation. Building began in 1173 and the tower started to sink once the second floor was under way. Work then paused for the better part of a century, and the tower was not finished until the 14th century. The tower is about 56 metres tall. After stabilisation work between 1993 and 2001 the tilt was reduced to just under four degrees. The whole square is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, declared in 1987. Keep the cathedral or some lawn in the frame so the lean has something to be measured against. The square is busy, so take a few shots and wait for a gap in the crowd. Check the horizon line before you press the shutter, because the tower is meant to look crooked and the ground should look level.
text.geographic_location: In Piazza del Duomo (Cathedral Square) in Pisa, Italy, standing next to Pisa Cathedral and the baptistery, about 700 m east of Pisa San Rossore railway station.
text.directions_text: Start from Pisa San Rossore railway station, the nearest station, which is 701 m west of the tower. If you arrive at Central Station of Pisa (railway station) instead, the tower is 1,690 m to the north, about 27 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole tower with a little space around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand closer and want the full height in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the arches and the bell chamber at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Duomo (east side of the lawn, about 15–20 m from the Tower base). The Tower leaning away from the camera, with the lawn in the foreground, for the classic forced-perspective 'holding up the Tower' photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and keep the horizon on a horizontal line, so the lean looks real rather than like a tilted phone. Hold the phone upright for the full height. Leave a strip of lawn at the bottom and some sky at the top. A bit of the cathedral beside the tower gives a useful comparison for the lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower's marble to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white stone keeps its detail against a bright sky. With ultra-wide, keep the tower in the middle of the frame, because the edges can stretch it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the marble and fewer people in the shot. Around midday the white stone can look flat and glary.

text.access_note: The square is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Access rules can change, so check locally before you visit.

name: Manarola, Cinque Terre
label: Manarola
camera_source: OpenStreetMap: Punta Bonfiglio (node 14206397146), the classic view back to the village; no Commons cluster was found.

text.description:
Manarola is one of the villages of the Cinque Terre, on the Ligurian coast in the province of La Spezia. That gap is useful. From a little distance you can fit the whole group of houses into one frame, with the sea and sky around it, instead of only seeing narrow lanes and doorways.

The village photographs well because the houses are colourful and packed closely together on the rocky coast, and the shapes read clearly even on a small screen. A wide frame shows the village in its setting, while a tighter zoom picks out roofs, shutters and washing lines. Take a few of each, because the two give quite different pictures.

The path and viewpoint areas around the village can be busy, so take your shots without blocking the way, and keep a firm hold of your phone near any drop or railing. Wipe the lens before you start, since sea air and pockets leave marks that show up as haze in bright light. If a path or viewpoint is closed or restricted, check the official site before you go.

It is worth strolling a little either side of it and checking the screen, because a few steps left or right can clear a railing or a signpost from the frame.
text.geographic_location: Manarola lies in the Cinque Terre on the Ligurian coast, in the Riomaggiore area of the province of La Spezia, Liguria.
text.directions_text: Start from Manarola railway station. The village is 208 m to the north-west of the station, about 3 minutes on foot. Check the official site before you go for the latest access to paths and viewpoints. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the village and its surroundings. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out groups of houses. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to a wall or railing and cannot step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Punta Bonfiglio (rocky promontory above the harbour; a few metres right of the main overlook for a higher, quieter angle). The pastel houses tumbling toward the small cove and harbour, with the sea filling the background. Keep a little distance rather than walking right up to the village, so the whole group of houses fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, so the sea does not slice the picture in half. Keep the houses on one of the side thirds and leave some sky or water for balance. Hold the phone level, because tilted buildings are easy to spot in a view like this.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the houses to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Wipe the lens first and take a few shots in case of movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light than midday, and fewer people on the paths. Check the screen as you go, because haze or low sun can change how the colours look.

text.access_note: Access to paths and viewpoints around the village may be restricted or subject to rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Trevi Fountain, Rome
label: Trevi Fountain
camera_source: Commons cluster (183 photos). Moved 15 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 5 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13448560: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trevi Fountain' (61 m across).

text.description:
The Trevi Fountain is a huge Baroque fountain built against the back of a palace, so it feels more like a stage set than a monument. Sculpted rock, columns and statues tumble down into a small square, and the central figure is Oceanus, riding a shell chariot guided by tritons and sea horses. It was designed by Nicola Salvi and finished by Giuseppe Pannini in 1762. It stands 26.3 metres high and 49.15 metres wide, which makes it the largest Baroque fountain in the world.

It photographs well because everything is packed into one frame: pale travertine, moving water and deep shadows between the columns. The square is small, so you are always close to a very big subject, and a phone's wide view helps. The name comes from the Latin for a meeting of three streets, and the fountain sits where three roads join.

A small detail worth finding is a sculpted vase that Romans call the "Ace of Cups". Salvi placed it to hide a barber's sign that he thought spoiled the view. After the 2014-2015 restoration, more than 100 LED lights were installed, so the fountain also looks good after dark.

Expect people in front of you. Use them for scale, or wait a moment for a gap. Keep your phone steady against your chest, and check your edges so the top of the palace and both side wings are not cut off.
text.geographic_location: The fountain is in the Trevi district of central Rome, set against the rear of the Palazzo Poli in a small square where three streets meet.
text.directions_text: Start from Barberini Metro station. The fountain is 543 m to the south-west, which is about 9 minutes on foot (Spagna Metro station is a little further, 657 m to the north of the fountain, about 11 minutes on foot). From Barberini, head south-west towards the phone icon on the map, which is on the east side of the small square. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole width of the fountain in the tight square. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the central figure of Oceanus and the sculpted rockwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take a few steps sideways for different angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the central niche on the middle line, with the palace roofline near the top third. Keep your phone level so the columns stay upright. Include some people at the water's edge to show how big the fountain is, or wait for a short gap in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright travertine and white water keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold still. Try a Live Photo to catch the water moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer for clear shots, and after dark the fountain is lit by its LED lighting. Midday is bright and harsh and tends to be busiest.

text.access_note: A ticketing system for approaching the fountain was introduced in February 2026, so check the official site before you go for current rules and times.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens is likely to be needed to fit the full width of the fountain from the stand-here point.
Early morning is usually less crowded at the Trevi Fountain.

name: Portofino

text.description:
Portofino is a small Italian Riviera village in the Metropolitan City of Genoa, built around a tiny harbour and lined with colourfully painted buildings. That is the whole appeal for a phone camera: a compact bowl of water, boats in the foreground and rows of painted houses climbing behind them, all in one frame. Look for the reflections of the façades in the water, and for the lines of moored boats, which lead the eye into the scene.

The name goes back a long way. Pliny the Elder wrote of Portus Delphini, the 'Port of the Dolphin', on this stretch of the Ligurian coast. The harbour supported fishing boats for centuries. From the late 19th century, British and then other Northern European visitors began arriving, and by 1950 tourism had replaced fishing as the town's main industry. Castello Brown dates from the 16th century. Underwater in the nearby inlet is the Christ of the Abyss statue, placed in 1954 at a depth of 17 metres. You won't photograph that one from the shore, but it is a nice detail to know.

For the best result, go to the phone icon on the map and look north-west towards the village. Take a few frames at different zoom levels rather than one, and keep an eye out for people walking into the shot along the waterfront. A quick wipe of your lens helps, as sea air can leave a haze on it.

name: Taormina and its Greek Theatre
label: Taormina
camera_source: Commons cluster (132 photos). Moved 52 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 55 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/42403497: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Greek theatre' (133 m across).

text.description:
Taormina's ancient theatre is a Greek-style theatre in Sicily, first built around the third century BC. It was rebuilt under Roman rule, probably around the time of Hadrian or Trajan, and altered again in the third century AD, when the orchestra became an arena and the stage was removed. That mix of layers gives the curved rows of seating a lot of character. The theatre is about 107 metres across and could once hold around 10,000 people. It is also one of the oldest theatres in Magna Graecia to have a curved seating area rather than the older trapezoid plan. Today it is a venue for the annual Taormina Film Festival, and you may recognise it from the 1995 film Mighty Aphrodite or from the second season of The White Lotus.

It photographs well because of the shapes. The sweep of the seating and the open backdrop beyond it pull the eye in. On a phone, think in layers: some stone in the foreground, the curve of the theatre in the middle, and the distant view behind. Walk a little to either side to change the angle, and take a few frames with and without people for scale. Keep the phone level so the tiers do not lean. Check the official site before you go, as access to the theatre itself may be ticketed or restricted.
text.geographic_location: In the town of Taormina, Sicily, Italy, about 1.1 km north-east of Taormina-Giardini railway station. The theatre is an ancient monument within the town itself.
text.directions_text: Start from Taormina-Giardini railway station. The theatre lies to the north-east of it, about 19 minutes on foot (about 1,145 m in a straight line). Once you are there, head for the theatre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the theatre. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole curve of seating in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as stonework and the rows of seats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (upper tiers of the cavea, shooting through the gap in the ruined stage wall). The theatre's stage ruins framed with the Ionian coast on one side and Mount Etna on the other.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tiers of seating with the horizontal lines so they stay straight. Put a bit of stone in the foreground, then leave the open view beyond as the backdrop. Try both portrait and landscape orientation: portrait for details, landscape for the whole sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the bright sky does not wash out. If your phone has panorama mode, move slowly and keep the phone level for a wide sweep of the seating.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon tends to give softer light and a more relaxed visit than midday. Check the official site for the times the theatre is open.

text.access_note: The theatre is a historic monument that may be ticketed or have restricted access, so check the official site before you go.

name: Florence Cathedral (the Duomo)
label: Florence Duomo
camera_source: Commons cluster (112 photos). Moved 77 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 95 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/43768260: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Santa Maria del Fiore' (184 m across).

text.description:
Florence Cathedral, formally Santa Maria del Fiore, is the great marble-clad church at the heart of the city's historic centre. Work began in 1296 and the dome was finished in 1436, engineered by Filippo Brunelleschi. The walls are faced in bands of white, green and pink marble. The ornate west front is much younger than the rest, a 19th-century design by Emilio De Fabris that was completed in 1887. The cathedral stands in Piazza del Duomo beside the Baptistery and Giotto's Campanile, and the three buildings are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site covering the historic centre.

It photographs well because of the colour and the scale. The patterned marble catches the light and gives your picture plenty of texture, and the dome rising behind the front gives the scene a clear shape. The sources describe it as one of the world's largest churches, and its dome as the largest masonry dome ever built. That size is the main challenge for a phone: you will not fit everything in at close range, so decide whether you want the whole building or a detail.

Stay a little back from the front so the lines do not lean too steeply. Take one wide shot, then move closer for pictures of the marble patterns and the carved doorways. Expect other visitors in the frame, so be patient and wait for a gap.
text.geographic_location: In Piazza del Duomo, in the historic centre of Florence, Tuscany, next to the Baptistery and Giotto's Campanile.
text.directions_text: Start from Firenze Santa Maria Novella railway station, the nearest station to the cathedral. The cathedral is 889 m from the station to the south-east, which is about 14 minutes on foot. The next nearest is Firenze Statuto railway station, 1,668 m to the north of the cathedral's south side, so Santa Maria Novella is the easier start. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full front of the building, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the marble patterns, the carved doors and the upper parts of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazzale Michelangelo (left side of the terrace, near the central balustrade). The classic panorama with the Duomo rising above the terracotta rooftops, the Arno, and the Ponte Vecchio, with Palazzo Vecchio's tower nearby. Then step a little closer if you want a tighter picture of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the vertical edges of the building so it does not look tilted. Keep the phone level and upright, and leave some sky above the top. For people-free shots, wait for a gap in the crowd, or use a gap in the foreground to frame the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the marble to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail. Hold the phone still with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the marble and fewer people in the square. After dark, night mode works well if the building is lit; brace your elbows to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: The square outside is open to walk around, but the cathedral is a working place of worship and some parts, such as the dome climb, may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: San Gimignano towers
label: San Gimignano
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/42458: large area 'San Gimignano' (20828 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
San Gimignano is a small walled hill town in the Tuscan province of Siena, and its group of medieval tower houses forms an unforgettable skyline. The towers rise above terracotta roofs and the town walls, and the hilltop setting means they stand out clearly against the sky. That is why this spot works so well on a phone: the shapes are bold and simple, and you don't need to be close to get a good picture.

The towers were built by rival families who competed to build higher. At the end of the Middle Ages there were 72 tower houses, some up to 70 metres tall. The council eventually ruled that none could be taller than the one next to the Palazzo Comunale. After the Black Death in 1348 the town came under Florence, and many towers were cut down to the height of the houses. About a dozen survive today, and the historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The phone icon on the map is about 95 m east of the subject. This gives you enough distance to fit several towers into one frame, with the town's rooftops below them. Look for a clear gap between the towers so the outlines don't merge into one lump. Keep your phone level so the towers stay upright, and take a few shots at slightly different zoom levels. Then pick the one with the cleanest sky around the tops.
text.geographic_location: San Gimignano is a walled hill town in Valdelsa, in the province of Siena, Tuscany.
text.directions_text: The nearest station given is Poggibonsi-San Gimignano railway station, about 8.7 km east of the towers, which is about 141 minutes on foot (Certaldo railway station is similar, at about 8.8 km to the north of the towers, or about 143 minutes on foot). That is a long walk, so you may prefer to continue from the station by local bus or by car; check current options locally before you go. Walk west towards them if you want a closer, more upward-looking view. The phone icon on the map is about 95 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole skyline. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a few towers and flatten the view. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close in a narrow street and want to fit a tower in from the base up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 95 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Place the tops of the towers in the upper third and leave the rooftops below them. Use a doorway, arch or tree branch at the edge of the frame to add depth, but keep the tower tops clear of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone doesn't wash out. If the sky is very bright, try a second shot with the slider up and compare them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good bet, as the sun is behind you and lights the faces of the towers. Late afternoon puts the sun in front of you, so expect backlight and silhouettes. Try these as a deliberate choice, and tap the sky to expose for it.

text.access_note: The town is a historic centre that you can walk around, but individual towers, churches and museums may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Milan Cathedral, known locally as the Duomo, is the cathedral church of Milan and the seat of the city's archbishop. It is the largest church in Italy and one of the largest in the world. That scale is why it photographs so well. The front and the crowd of spires fill the frame, and the pale stone stands out against the sky. Building began in 1386 and took nearly six centuries, with the last details finished in 1965. The Gothic style came partly from French engineers called in during the early years. Look for the small Renaissance spire known as the Guglietto dell'Amadeo, built between 1507 and 1510. It sits comfortably among the Gothic pinnacles and is a good target for a close-up. The Duomo stands on the site of earlier churches. An early Christian baptistery, dated to 335, can be visited beneath it. Take a few frames with different framing: one wide shot of the whole front, one at a slight angle, and one detail of the spires. Check the edges of the screen so people's heads or bags do not cut into the corners. Wipe your lens first, as pocket dust softens a bright, pale subject.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Milan, in Lombardy, Italy, at the heart of the old city, where the streets either radiate from the cathedral or circle it.
text.directions_text: Start from Duomo Metro station, the nearest station, which is about 175 m from the cathedral, with the cathedral to the east. That is about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Duomo (western half of the square, slightly left of centre when facing the cathedral). The full white marble façade filling the frame, with the Galleria entrance in the left foreground and the main spire with the Madonnina centred above. Take a few steps left or right to change the angle and avoid people in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central axis with the middle grid line. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines do not lean. Leave some sky above the spires. For a second shot, step to one side and use the 1x lens for a slight angle. For a third, zoom in on the spires at 3x or 5x.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames. In the evening, use night mode and keep still for the full count.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the stonework. After dark, night mode can work well if the building is lit.

text.access_note: The Duomo is a place of worship, so check the official site for access and visiting details before you go.

name: Sassi di Matera
label: Matera
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Sassi di Matera'.

text.description:
The Sassi di Matera are two old districts of the city, Sasso Caveoso and Sasso Barisano, where houses and lanes are cut into and stacked up the soft pale rock of a ravine. The streets in some places run across the roofs of other homes, so the whole slope looks like one continuous, layered honeycomb of stone. That is what makes it so good with a phone: you get repeating shapes, warm stone colours and a deep drop into the valley all in one frame.

People have lived here for a very long time. There is evidence of settlement as far back as 7000 BC, which makes the Sassi one of the earliest known settlements in Italy. UNESCO named them a World Heritage Site in 1993, together with the park of the Rupestrian Churches. In the 1950s most residents were moved out to newer parts of the city, and today the area has been revived with hotels, pubs and other businesses.

Take a first shot wide to show the scale of the hillside, then step in and look for a smaller scene: a doorway, a stairway or a line of chimneys. Include a bit of foreground, such as a wall or railing, to give the picture depth. Paving here is uneven and sloping, so watch your footing when you are looking at the screen.
text.geographic_location: In Matera, in the Basilicata region of southern Italy. The Sassi form the old town, on the slope of the Gravina ravine, alongside the Civita and the Piano.
text.directions_text: Start from Matera Centrale railway station, where the Sassi are 591 m to the east, about 10 minutes on foot. Matera Sud railway station is another option: the Sassi are 779 m to the north-east, about 13 minutes on foot. Walk slowly, as the lanes and steps slope and can be uneven. The phone icon on the map is about 250 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall view of the hillside. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to a wall or terrace and want more of the scene. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops, doorways and cave openings across the ravine.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 250 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the skyline of the houses on the upper third line, so the layered stone gets most of the frame. Keep a railing, wall or edge of the terrace at the bottom of the shot for depth. Check that the verticals look straight and that no one's head cuts across the main view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale rock keeps its texture and the sky does not go white. For a wide sweep along the ravine, try panorama mode and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening usually gives warm light on the stone. At dusk, when the lights come on, night mode can capture the glow on the hillside. Hold the phone still against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The Sassi are streets and districts of a living town, but individual churches, museums and cave houses may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Piazza del Campo, Siena
label: Piazza del Campo
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5965021: 'Fonte Gaia', the best-known feature inside 'Il Campo' (197 m across).

text.description:
Piazza del Campo is the main public square of Siena's historic centre, and it is shaped like a scallop shell that slopes gently down towards the Palazzo Pubblico and its tall Torre del Mangia. That gentle bowl is what makes it so good to photograph. The red brick is divided into nine wedges by pale stone lines, each filled with a herringbone pattern, so the ground itself gives you strong lines that lead the eye across the frame. The surrounding palazzi have matching rooflines and warm brick-and-stucco colours, which keeps pictures looking calm and balanced.

The square was paved in 1349, and the nine wedges are held to stand for the Nine who governed Siena at the time. It measures roughly 425 by 650 feet (about 130 by 200 metres), big enough to hold the whole city's population when it was built. Visitors often sit on the bricks as if on a lawn, which adds life and a sense of scale to a shot. The Fonte Gaia, dating from 1419, sits at the north-west edge. The twice-yearly Palio horse race is run around the edge of the square.

For your phone, stand at the phone icon on the map and look north-east across the square. Include some of the brick pattern in the foreground, keep the rooflines level, and let people sit in the frame to show how big the space is.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Siena's historic centre in Tuscany, inside Piazza del Campo (Il Campo) at the foot of the Palazzo Pubblico and its Torre del Mangia. The subject, Fonte Gaia, is the best-known feature of the square.
text.directions_text: Start from Siena railway station and walk south-east into the historic centre to Piazza del Campo, about 26 minutes on foot. Go to the phone icon on the map. From there the subject (Fonte Gaia) is 48 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the shell-shaped square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the top of the tower or the rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the stone dividing lines so they lead into the picture, keeping the rooflines level. Put a few people sitting on the bricks in the frame to give a sense of scale. For a tall shot of the tower, tilt your phone up only slightly, so the walls don't lean inwards too much.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick or the facades to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Try panorama mode for the full curve of the square, moving slowly and keeping your phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, and late afternoon tends to give warmer light on the brick. The square is very busy on Palio days, so check the official site for event dates before you go.

text.access_note: Piazza del Campo is an open public square, but access may change on event days such as the Palio, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ponte Vecchio, Florence
label: Ponte Vecchio
camera_source: Commons cluster (31 photos). Moved 13 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 130 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5342094: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ponte Vecchio' (126 m across).

text.description:
The Ponte Vecchio, or "Old Bridge", is a medieval stone bridge over the Arno, lined with small shops that hang out over the water. It is the only bridge in Florence that was not destroyed in World War II, and today it is considered the city's oldest. The shops were first used by butchers, tanners and farmers. Since a decree of 1565, only goldsmiths and jewellers have been allowed, and today you will also find art dealers and souvenir sellers. The Vasari Corridor, built in 1565 to link the Palazzo Vecchio with the Palazzo Pitti, runs above part of the bridge.

From upriver you can see the back shops (retrobotteghe), the jumbled, projecting rooms added in the seventeenth century. They make a more interesting picture than the busy street front. The three shallow arches, the largest spanning 30 m, sit in a neat row above their reflection when the water is calm.

On a phone, the bridge looks small and distant from here, so do not rely on the default lens (1x) alone. Zoom in until the bridge fills the width of the frame, and keep the river in the lower third so the arches and reflections show. Take a few shots, because walkers and boats move through the scene and the light changes quickly.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Florence, Tuscany, crossing the Arno at its narrowest point. It lies between the Ponte Santa Trinita and the Ponte alle Grazie.
text.directions_text: Start from Firenze Santa Maria Novella railway station. The bridge is about 1157 m to the south-east, which is about 19 minutes on foot. Follow the river westwards from the phone icon on the map to reach the bridge. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to check the scene, then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the bridge closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the bridge a thin strip in the distance, so use it only for a sweeping river-and-sky view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Keep a clear view of the arches and the stacked back shops, and stay out of the way of other walkers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge along the upper-middle line, with the water in the lower third. Zoom until the bridge spans most of the frame, then include a little of the river bank on one side to give a sense of scale. For a calmer picture, wait for a gap between passing boats or people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the buildings stay detailed. Try a Live Photo, which lets you pick the best frame once boats or walkers have moved. At dusk, night mode can help, but hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the warm stonework and the water. A calm early hour also tends to mean fewer people in the foreground. At dusk the bridge lights can reflect in the river, so stay on for a few frames.

name: Faraglioni of Capri
label: Capri
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4193334177: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Faraglioni are rock stacks just off the coast of Capri. The Faraglioni sit by Via Camerelle, on Capri, in the Napoli province of Campania.

They photograph well because the shapes are bold and simple. Dark rock against blue sea and sky makes a clear picture even on a small screen. At this range the stacks will not fill the frame on the default lens (1x), so plan on using some zoom, and let the sea, the cliffs and any boats add scale. A gap of empty sky above the rocks gives the picture room to breathe.

Be realistic about the view. Distant detail softens when you zoom a lot, so take a few frames at different zoom levels and keep the best. Hold the phone with both hands and rest your elbows against your body or a wall to keep it steady. If the path is busy, wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or use them as scale on purpose. Take care near edges and drops, and follow any local signs.
text.geographic_location: On the coast of Capri (Napoli, Campania), close to Via Camerelle.
text.directions_text: Start from Piazza Umberto I (Funicolare di Capri), a funicular station. The Faraglioni lie about 369 m to the east of it, which is about 6 minutes on foot. Marina Grande (Funicolare di Capri), also a funicular station, is further away: the rocks lie about 931 m to the south-east of it, about 15 minutes on foot. From either station, head for the phone icon on the map. From there the Faraglioni lie about 478 m to the south, so face south and look out over the water. Allow extra time on arrival to find a clear spot to stand. The phone icon on the map is about 480 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) for a wide establishing shot with plenty of sea and sky. Then move to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the rocks closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, because it will make the rocks look very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 480 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the rocks on one of the vertical lines, leaving open sea in front of them. Keep the horizon level using the grid. Try one wide frame with a foreground such as a railing, plants or the cliff edge, and one tighter zoomed frame of just the stacks.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rocks to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the rock does not wash out. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, and avoid going past about 5x if the image looks soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light and fewer people. Midday sun can look harsh and flat, and the rocks may be partly backlit when you shoot south.

text.access_note: Check the official site or local signs before you go, as access to viewpoints and paths in this area may vary.

name: St Mark's Square, Venice
label: St Mark's Square
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/172349507: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Mark's Square' (280 m across).

text.description: St Mark's Square is the main public square of Venice, and locals simply call it la Piazza. Together with the smaller Piazzetta that runs down towards the water, it forms the social, religious and political centre of the city. It photographs well because everything is arranged around one long open space. St Mark's Basilica closes the eastern end, long arcaded buildings run down both sides, and the Campanile stands free of them. The basilica's western front has great arches and marble decoration, with Romanesque carvings around the central doorway, and four horses that preside over the whole piazza. The Clocktower, completed in 1499, sits over the archway leading to the Merceria shopping street. The Campanile was rebuilt in 1912 exactly as it was, after the old one collapsed on 14 July 1902. Three tall flagpoles in front of the church have bronze bases carved in 1505. Caffè Florian, opened in 1720, sits under the arcade on the south side. For photos, the arcades make strong repeating lines that lead the eye to the basilica, and the flagpoles and clocktower give you foreground and detail shots. The square is big, so try a wide view first, then move in on one feature at a time. Expect people in almost every frame, and use them to show the scale of the place.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Venice, at the head of the Piazzetta that opens onto the St Mark's basin of the lagoon. The basilica stands at the eastern end of the square, which is about 280 m across.
text.directions_text: Start from Venezia Santa Lucia railway station, the nearest station given for this spot. The middle of St Mark's Square is about 25 minutes on foot from the station, to the south-east of it. The phone icon on the map is about 1 minute on foot from the middle of the square, and the square's centre lies to the south-west of it. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full length of the square and its arcades. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view with less stretching at the edges. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clocktower, the carvings and the flagpole bases.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the arcade lines running neatly towards the edges of the frame. Keep your phone level so the tall buildings do not lean. Leave some open paving at the bottom to show how large the square is, and try a second shot with a flagpole or an arch in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building facades to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. In the evening, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady. For a sweep of the whole square, try panorama mode and turn slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the frame, and the buildings often look good in soft light. Dusk is worth trying with night mode once the lights come on.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the basilica, the Campanile and the museums around it have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter in the square.
Soft early light and dusk lighting often suit the buildings.
The square is busy with people throughout much of the day.

name: Trulli of Alberobello
label: Alberobello
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/40749: large area 'Alberobello' (13055 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Alberobello is a small town in Apulia, and its trulli are the reason people come. These are round, whitewashed stone houses topped with cone-shaped roofs made of stacked limestone slabs. Seen together on a slope, the grey cones make a repeating pattern that suits a phone camera well. The trulli of Alberobello have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996, and the town is the only inhabited place with a whole district of them.

The building style has a practical history. The local counts required houses to be built from dry stone, with no mortar, so they could be treated as temporary buildings that were easy to pull down. The builders found that a round, self-supporting domed roof was the simplest answer. Many roofs carry a small decorative pinnacle on top, which was a kind of signature of the master builder. Look for these when you zoom in, because they make good details.

Take the first shot from the marked point to show the scale of the roofs. Then walk towards them and look for lanes where the cones stack up behind each other. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the white walls do not lean. People live here, so keep your voice down and do not step into doorways or private terraces.
text.geographic_location: Alberobello is a small town in the Metropolitan City of Bari, in Apulia, in southern Italy.
text.directions_text: Start at Alberobello railway station. The trulli area is about 493 m to the south-west, which is about 8 minutes on foot. That is about 4 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 260 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) at the phone icon on the map to show the roofs in their setting. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cones and pinnacles. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only in the narrow lanes, and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 260 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the roof line on the upper third. Let one or two cones sit in the foreground so the rest repeat behind them. When you are close, frame a single roof with its pinnacle against the sky, or look along a lane so the walls lead the eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a white wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the whitewash keeps its texture and the sky does not turn white. At 2x or more, hold the phone steady with both hands, or brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the streets are likely to be quieter. Midday sun can make the white walls too bright.

text.access_note: The trulli district is a part of a living town; check the official site before you go for any restrictions on particular buildings or visits inside them.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light than midday.
Streets in the trulli district are likely to be quieter early in the day.
Bright white walls can fool a phone's exposure and make the sky look washed out.
Some individual trulli may be private homes or shops with their own access rules.
The stand-here point is on the southern side of the trulli district, so pointing north faces the subject.

name: Grand Canal and Rialto Bridge, Venice
label: Rialto Bridge
camera_source: Commons cluster (45 photos). Moved 37 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 290 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2289364: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rialto Bridge' (84 m across).

text.description:
The Rialto Bridge is the oldest of the four bridges that cross the Grand Canal in Venice, linking the districts of San Marco and San Polo. The stone bridge you see today was designed by Antonio da Ponte and built between 1588 and 1591. It is a single broad arch with two ramps climbing to a central portico, and the covered ramps on either side are lined with rows of shops. The design was so bold that the architect Vincenzo Scamozzi predicted it would fail, yet it has stood for more than four centuries. Before it, a series of bridges stood on the spot, starting with a pontoon bridge in the 12th century and later a wooden one that collapsed more than once.

It photographs well because the pale single arch sits right over the water, with boats passing beneath and old buildings along both banks. Expect the bridge to look fairly small at the default lens (1x), so use the zoom to bring it closer. Then walk on to the bridge itself for a second set of pictures looking along the canal. The area is popular, so take your time, keep your phone close to you and be ready for people walking into the frame.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Venice, northern Italy, where the bridge crosses the Grand Canal between the San Marco and San Polo districts, about 1.2 km east of Venezia Santa Lucia railway station.
text.directions_text: Start from Venezia Santa Lucia railway station, the nearest station to the spot. The Rialto Bridge is 1,210 metres to the east, about 20 minutes on foot. Head east on foot and keep the Grand Canal in view as you approach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from where you stand, because the bridge is 293 metres away. The default lens (1x) gives a wider view of the canal and buildings. Save the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you are close to the bridge or on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Riva del Ferro (east bank, in front of Hotel Rialto, on the wooden docks). The arch of the Rialto Bridge across the Grand Canal, with the canal and any passing gondola or boat in the frame. Then walk the 5 minutes or so to the bridge for close-up shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge on one of the lower thirds, with the water filling the foreground. Keep the canal edges roughly straight so the buildings do not lean. At the bridge, try a wide shot along the canal with the arch at one side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Live Photos can catch passing boats, and night mode helps after dark if you rest your phone on a ledge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the soft light at the start or end of the day tends to flatter the stonework and the water.

text.access_note: The bridge connects the San Marco and San Polo districts.

Early morning is usually quieter at popular Venice landmarks.
Soft light at the start or end of the day tends to flatter stonework and water.
The area around the Rialto Bridge is popular with visitors and can be crowded.
